blocks.p: Consumer advocate Clark Howard flagged the pattern again recently: cable broadband promotional pricing commonly starts around $50/month in year one, steps up to about $85 in month 13, and passes $95 by year three. A small business on autopay that never opens the bill can end up paying roughly $840 more over two years than the promotional price suggested (24/7 Wall St. estimate). Charter and Comcast each lost roughly 170,000 broadband subscribers in a single recent quarter — the customers who leave are saving money. The ones who stay and never look at the bill are subsidizing them.

blocks.h: Find your promo end date before it finds you

blocks.p: On Xfinity's 400 Mbps plan, for example, a $55/month promotional rate reverts to about $95/month after 12 months. Since 2024, the FCC has required providers to hand you a Broadband Label at signup that lists the standard rate that applies after the promotion ends. Find that label — or the promotional-discount line on a recent bill — and you will know exactly what your bill becomes, and when.

blocks.h: Prefer flat-rate fiber where you can get it

blocks.p: AT&T Fiber, Google Fiber, Frontier, and T-Mobile Home Internet generally use flat-rate pricing: the first bill and the twenty-fourth bill cost the same. Fiber has a second advantage in an office — symmetric speeds. Cable plans advertised at 1.25 Gbps down often deliver only 35–50 Mbps up, which chokes cloud backups and large uploads for everyone in the office at the worst possible time.

blocks.h: Stop renting the modem

ul: Provider modem/router rentals run $10–$20/month — $120–$240 a year, every year.
A compatible modem plus a business-grade router typically pays for itself in about 18 months.
One caution: running a 20-person office on a consumer router is a false economy. When it exhausts its connection table, the savings come back as dropped calls and reboot cycles.

blocks.h: When business-class service is worth the premium

blocks.p: Comcast Business, for example, runs roughly $60–$170/month for 300 Mbps to 2 Gbps service (business.org, October 2026), with no data caps, business support, and service-level commitments; a five-year price lock is available for about $20/month more on a one-year term. The decision rule is arithmetic: if one hour of downtime costs your business more than about $100, business-class service pays for itself. If an outage is an inconvenience rather than a loss, residential fiber plus a backup connection is often the smarter spend.

blocks.h: Put the expiry date on a calendar

blocks.p: Two to three weeks before a promotion expires, call the provider, ask for a retention offer, and mention the competing fiber quote while you do it. Providers routinely renew promotional pricing for customers who ask. They almost never volunteer it for customers who don't.

articles.summary: Promotional pricing quietly expires, autopay hides the increase, and two years later a small office has overpaid by hundreds of dollars. How the pricing ladder works, and how to avoid it.
articles.title: Why Your Business Internet Bill Jumps After Month 12 — and How to Stop Overpaying

blocks.p: On October 20, 2026, a power fault in Google Cloud's europe-west2-b zone in London interrupted Revolut's payments and app across seven countries. Hyperscalers spend billions on redundancy and can still be taken down by a power event. A small facility cannot outspend that problem — but it can refuse the cheapest single points of failure, starting with the core switch.

blocks.h: One core switch is a decision, not a default

blocks.p: A MikroTik CRS518 — with 2×100G and 16×25G ports — lists at $1,595. A pair running MLAG costs a little over $3,000. Weigh that against one core failure: Uptime Institute's 2026 outage analysis attributes 23% of IT-service-related outages to network and connectivity issues, and 52% of major outages cost between $100,000 and $1 million each. At those numbers, a second core switch is not an upgrade. It is insurance with a very small premium.

blocks.h: Stacking is not redundancy

blocks.p: Stacked switches present as one logical device, which is exactly the problem: they share a control plane, so a stack-master failure or a stack-link fault shakes the whole unit. MLAG keeps two independent control planes that synchronize state — one box can lose power entirely and the other keeps forwarding, with no reconvergence event your customers can feel. If redundancy is written into your SLA, MLAG is the version you can defend.

blocks.h: Do the oversubscription math before you buy

blocks.p: An access switch with 48×1G ports can offer at most 48 Gbps. At a 3:1 oversubscription ratio, the design point is 16 Gbps of uplink — in practice, 2×10G LACP provides 20 Gbps (2.4:1) with sensible headroom. Under-provision the uplinks and the evening peak saturates them while customers complain; over-provision and you have paid for ports that will never light up. The ratio is the decision. The hardware follows from it.

blocks.h: Review power and network on the same sheet

blocks.p: The London incident was a power fault, not a network fault — but the network is always what customers notice first. A redundancy review that covers only switches misses the point: dual utility feeds, UPS runtime, and generator test results belong on the same one-page checklist as core redundancy.

articles.summary: A power fault at Google Cloud's London region took Revolut's payments down across seven countries. For small facilities, the relevant lesson is how much still hangs off a single core switch — and what fixing that actually costs.
articles.title: Core Switch Redundancy in Small Data Centers: MLAG, Oversubscription, and the Cost of One Box

blocks.p: In October 2024, attackers breached the network of Washington Gastroenterology, a practice with 19 locations in the Tacoma area. Data belonging to roughly 583,000 people was exposed, and the resulting class action settled for $4.6 million. Figures like that are usually associated with hospital systems, not regional practices — which is exactly why this case matters to small businesses: attackers do not check your revenue before they check your defenses.

blocks.h: What a settlement covers — and what it doesn't

blocks.p: A settlement pays for claims, notification, and credit monitoring. It does not pay for weeks of disrupted scheduling, the staff hours consumed by response and audits, or the patients who quietly take their records elsewhere. For a small organization, the operational damage routinely exceeds the legal bill.

blocks.h: The controls that decide whether a breach stays small

blocks.p: None of the following requires an enterprise budget. Together, they decide whether one compromised password becomes an incident report or a headline:

ul: Multi-factor authentication on every remote-access path and every admin account — with no exceptions for 'temporary' accounts.
Network segmentation: guest Wi-Fi, payment systems, office workstations, and IoT devices (cameras, printers, TVs) on separate VLANs, so one compromised device is not a skeleton key.
Patching on a schedule: firewalls, VPN appliances, and servers updated routinely. Internet-facing edge devices are the most common way in.
3-2-1 backups: three copies, on two different media, one offsite or immutable — and a restore that has actually been tested. A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a backup.
Offboarding hygiene: departed employees' accounts disabled the same day, and vendor access reviewed every quarter.

blocks.h: The question to ask this week

blocks.p: If your office manager, your front desk, and your bookkeeper all work on the same flat network as the waiting-room TV, a single phishing click has a path to everything you hold. Segmentation and MFA at small-business scale are a few hundred dollars of configuration work. The expensive way to learn that is from a settlement headline with your name in it.

articles.summary: Washington Gastroenterology — 19 locations in the Tacoma area — settled a class action for $4.6 million after an October 2024 breach exposed the data of about 583,000 people. The lessons apply to any small business that holds customer data.
articles.title: A $4.6 Million Settlement: What a Washington Clinic's Data Breach Teaches Small Businesses

blocks.p: When Square's platform went down for about 14 hours, affected merchants discovered how much of a modern shop runs through a single connection: card payments, online orders, receipt printers, even the phone system. One Internet line is a single point of failure for all of it. The remedy is well understood and cheaper than most owners expect — a second connection, from a different provider on a different medium, with automatic failover.

blocks.h: What 'backup Internet' actually means

ul: Two independent circuits: cable plus fiber, or cable plus 5G. Two lines from the same provider, on the same pole, are not redundancy.
A dual-WAN router or firewall that detects a failure and switches automatically. Nobody should be unplugging cables during the lunch rush.
A realistic bandwidth floor: the backup only has to carry payments, phones, and essential cloud apps. A 5G connection that would feel slow for the whole office is plenty for the register.

blocks.h: The 3-minute self-check when things go down

blocks.p: Order matters. First, check whether the provider itself is down — a status page, or a phone on cellular data — before rebooting anything. Second, if you do reboot, go in order: modem or ONT first, wait for full sync, then the router, then switches. Third, if payments are down but the connection is clearly up, suspect the payment platform, not your network. The Square outage fooled thousands of owners into rebooting perfectly healthy equipment.

blocks.h: What continuity costs

blocks.p: A business 5G backup connection typically runs $50–$110/month, and a dual-WAN firewall for a small office is a one-time cost in the low hundreds. Set that against one day of card-paying customers walking out the door. Business continuity is no longer an enterprise feature; it is a line item smaller than the coffee budget.

articles.summary: A roughly 14-hour Square outage left merchants unable to take card payments for most of a business day. The fix is not a bigger plan — it is a second, independent connection that fails over automatically.
articles.title: When the Registers Stop: A Backup Internet Playbook for Small Businesses
Small Data Center Power Redundancy: UPS Sizing, Generator Testing, and Battery Safety Checklist
articles.summary: A UPS battery fire shut down 647 government systems for 95 days. This guide turns that failure into an implementable checklist: size UPS runtime from measured load, run NFPA 110 generator load tests, choose N+1 vs 2N by downtime budget, and handle batteries without creating the next fire.

blocks.p: On the evening of September 26, 2025, a lithium-ion UPS battery caught fire while workers were moving it inside the National Information Resources Service (NIRS) data center in Daejeon, South Korea. Seventy systems went down first; to stop servers from overheating, operators then cut power proactively, and 647 government systems stopped in one night. Full recovery took 95 days. The lesson is not "buy more batteries." Every failure point in that chain was a procedure someone could have checked in advance. This is that checklist.

blocks.h: 1. Size UPS runtime from measured load, not the nameplate

blocks.p: A UPS nameplate tells you what the unit could do when new. It does not tell you what your load does at 2 p.m. on a busy day. Most UPS units at full load only carry 10-15 minutes, and a diesel generator still needs minutes to start and accept load. Plan for 15 minutes of real runtime, and prove it.

ul: Measure real load: read UPS output load percentage and kilowatts from its panel or monitoring for a full week, including peak. Size from the peak, not the average.

Worked example: 10 kW of peak load x 15 minutes = 2.5 kWh of usable energy. Divide by inverter efficiency (about 0.92) and the battery bank must be at least 2.7 kWh. Repeat the arithmetic with your own peak number.

Test quarterly: during a planned off-hours window, cut utility power and time the actual runtime. Replace the bank when measured runtime falls below your 15-minute target, not when a battery finally fails.

blocks.h: 2. Load-test the generator every month, on the books

blocks.p: A generator that has never carried real load is a rumor, not a backup. NFPA 110 sets the floor for emergency power testing, and the test only counts if it is written down.

ul: Run monthly: 30 minutes at no less than 30% of nameplate load, on building load or a load bank.
If building load cannot reach 30%, schedule an annual supplemental load-bank test (commonly 50% load for 30 minutes plus 75% load for 60 minutes).
Log four things every test: time from start to load acceptance, load percentage, coolant, oil and fuel readings, and any alarms. A test without a log did not happen.
Exercise the transfer switch too: Uptime Institute's 2026 outage analysis puts transfer-switch failures at 34% of power-related outages. Test the switch, not just the engine.

blocks.h: 3. Choose N+1 vs 2N by downtime budget, not by prestige

blocks.p: Both designs are legitimate; they buy different things. The honest way to choose is to start from the downtime your customer contracts can tolerate.

ul: N+1: one spare for each critical component type. It survives any single failure and costs far less, but shared paths remain — one switchboard fault can still take you down.
2N: two fully independent power trains. It survives the loss of an entire path, but you are essentially building a second power train, so the premium is large.

Decision rule: Tier III allows roughly 1.6 hours of downtime a year; Tier IV allows roughly 26 minutes. If your contracts tolerate hours, N+1 with disciplined maintenance is the honest choice. Buy 2N only when the penalty for minutes of downtime exceeds the build premium.

blocks.h: 4. Treat battery moves as hot work

blocks.p: The Daejeon fire started during a routine battery move, and three details made it catastrophic: the battery was at 80-90% charge when moved, while manufacturers recommend a low or medium charge before moving; the battery sat about 60 cm from the servers it powered; and there was no separation between the two. Fix all three before anyone touches a battery again.

ul: Before any battery move: discharge to the manufacturer's recommended level, disconnect main and auxiliary power, and confirm zero energy with a meter.
Separate batteries from IT gear: a dedicated battery room or rated separation. A battery fire next to servers becomes a data-center fire.

Watch temperature and age: VRLA batteries are rated about 10-12 years at 20 C, and every 10 C above that roughly halves life. Log battery-room temperature monthly, and replace banks that pass their rated life instead of waiting for a failure.

blocks.h: A maintenance calendar you can copy

ul: Monthly: generator load test, transfer-switch exercise, battery-room temperature log.
Quarterly: UPS runtime test and alarm/monitoring check.
Annually: supplemental load-bank test if needed, full battery inspection, and a review of the single-line diagram against what is actually installed.

blocks.p: Uptime Institute's 2026 outage analysis found power issues behind more than one in five IT service outages over the past three years, with UPS failures at 39%, transfer-switch failures at 34%, and generator failures at 28%. Every item above is a check someone can sign. That is the whole point: power redundancy is a maintenance discipline, not a purchase.

articles.title: When Primary and Backup Share One Cable: A Small Data Center Interconnect Checklist
articles.summary: A Lumen fiber cut took DentalXChange's primary and backup circuits down together for 15 hours — because both rode the same cable. Four checks that separate real redundancy from paper redundancy: physical path, BGP multi-homing, 95th-percentile billing, and outage cost math.

blocks.p: On the morning of December 10, 2025, monitoring at DentalXChange, a US data center services provider, lit up first: an upstream Lumen fiber segment in Santa Fe Springs, California, had been cut, affecting more than 800 cables. The worst part: DentalXChange's primary and backup internet circuits ran over that same segment — primary and backup went down together.

The provider rerouted logically, routes flapped across the network all day, and customers saw intermittent outages. Around midday, the team evaluated failing over to the Phoenix disaster-recovery site, only to find that the DR site rode the same unstable upstream paths — failing over would have been riskier, so they abandoned it. Service was not truly restored until the fiber was repaired at 8:24 PM, more than 15 hours later. The first item on the post-incident remediation list was BGP multi-homing with blended internet.

The lesson for small data center operators is not “fiber gets cut” — fiber always gets cut. It is that two circuits on a contract do not mean two paths. The single point of failure is usually not in the contract; it is in the trench. Four checks you can run against your own facility:

blocks.h: 1. Check the physical path, not the contract

blocks.p: Ask each carrier for a fiber route map and compare three points: does it enter the building through the same entrance, run through the same municipal conduit, and enter the data hall through the same tray? Any overlap is a single point of failure. That is exactly where DentalXChange failed: two circuits on paper, one cable in the ground. Re-verify route maps periodically — municipal construction and carrier mergers can quietly change your path.

blocks.h: 2. BGP multi-homing is what makes failover real

blocks.p: Get your own ASN and IP space, and announce to two or more upstreams: when one goes down, routing moves automatically, with no manual DNS changes and no VPN tunnels to rebuild. The bar is not high: an IPv4 /24 is generally the smallest block accepted for global announcement, and a facility with a few dozen racks can do it. Before signing, ask one question: is failover automatic, or does it wait for an engineer to switch it manually? Manual “redundancy” is no redundancy at 3 AM.

blocks.h: 3. The 95th-percentile billing trap is in the burst days

blocks.p: Carriers sample every 5 minutes — 8,640 samples a month — drop the top 5% (432 samples), and bill on the highest remaining value. A few hours of backups, a promotion, or a crawler surge can lift the whole month's bill one tier. Don't negotiate on headline price alone: TeleGeography Q2 2026 data puts the lowest 100G port price in the most competitive markets at $0.03/Mbps/month; Equinix's US example for 100 Mbps runs about $348/month, with overage at $5.22/Mbps. Staggering backup windows and rate-limiting them beats haggling after the fact.

blocks.h: 4. Price an outage as penalties plus losses

blocks.p: Uptime Institute's 2026 global survey: 71% of operators said their most severe outage in the past year cost at least $100,000, and 19% put it above $1 million. Fifteen hours down means SLA credits, churned customers, and overnight repair labor — none of it cheap. Moscow's M9 hub told the same story in August 2026: a power failure affected 467 networks, and 35% of them lost more than 90% of their routes — networks that were logically independent were physically packed into one building.

When a carrier tells you “we have redundancy,” ask one more question: redundancy through which trench? Redundancy you can't trace on a route map is paper redundancy. Redundancy isn't bought; it's verified.

articles.title: AI Inference Hosting Network Implementation Guide for Small Data Centers: RoCEv2 Fabric, Traffic Isolation, and Per-Row Power and Cooling
articles.summary: Inference hosting almost never needs InfiniBand. For a small data center at up to about 128 GPUs, tuned RoCEv2 lossless Ethernet is the cost-optimal fabric — if you separate the four traffic classes, tune the lossless parameters, and count one row's power and cooling before signing the customer.

blocks.p: This guide applies to small data centers (tens to hundreds of racks) offering AI inference hosting, including light fine-tuning. It reaches three conclusions: first, at up to about 128 GPUs, well-tuned RoCEv2 lossless Ethernet is the cost-optimal choice; second, four traffic classes must be separated; third, per-row power and cooling must be accounted for before signing a customer.

blocks.h: 1. Scope and prerequisites

blocks.p: Scope: small data centers (tens to hundreds of racks); workload: AI inference hosting, including light fine-tuning.
Out of scope: large multi-node training clusters; fabric selection for training requires separate evaluation.
Prerequisites: an operations team capable of tuning Ethernet; per-row electrical and cooling accounting data for the facility.

blocks.h: 2. Design principles

ul: Ethernet first: inference traffic mostly stays inside the node (NVLink); across nodes, high-speed Ethernet is sufficient. Tune the stack the team already runs; do not adopt a new stack for an unverified scenario.
Traffic isolation: four traffic classes must not share a congested link.
Power and cooling first: power and cooling are hard constraints; accounting comes before signing.

blocks.h: 3. Selection criteria: RoCEv2 vs. InfiniBand

ul: Applicable scale: RoCEv2 up to about 128 GPUs; InfiniBand for large multi-node training.
Cost structure: RoCEv2 reuses Ethernet operations capability at low incremental cost; InfiniBand requires dedicated hardware and operations capability at a high premium.

Adoption condition: adopt InfiniBand only when training time directly drives revenue and measurements verify a latency bottleneck that tuned RoCEv2 cannot close; use RoCEv2 for all other inference hosting scenarios.

blocks.h: 4. Implementation steps
4.1 Separate the fabrics

blocks.p: Four traffic classes: front-end requests, back-end GPU synchronization, storage (checkpoint and dataset reads), and management. Requirement: keep the back-end GPU fabric, storage, front-end, and management physically or logically separate; adopt a leaf-spine topology; complete structured fiber and optics deployment once to avoid later rebuilds.

blocks.h: 4.2 Configure lossless Ethernet

blocks.p: RoCEv2 lossless operation requires the following parameter set: PFC (Priority Flow Control), ECN, DCQCN congestion control, 9000-byte MTU, deep-buffer switches. Without tuning, RoCE performs no better than plain TCP. NVIDIA Spectrum-X follows the same Ethernet path, integrating per-packet adaptive routing and congestion control into the switch and NIC, which validates the Ethernet approach provided congestion control is implemented.

blocks.h: 4.3 Account for per-row power and cooling

blocks.p: Power and cooling are the first hard constraints for a small facility and must be calculated for one row before signing a customer. Per Uptime Institute's 2025 survey (786 operators): most respondents consider direct liquid cooling necessary above 20 kW per rack; the largest group placed air cooling's limit at 40–49 kW; the typical rack drew under 9 kW. NVIDIA's GB200 NVL72 rack requires about 120 kW, liquid-cooled — more than 13 times the typical rack. The International Energy Agency's 2026 report states AI server power density rose 11-fold between 2020 and 2025.

ul: Under 20 kW per rack: contained hot/cold aisles with air cooling remain viable.
20–75 kW: rear-door heat exchangers as the transitional tier (Motivair rates its ChilledDoor at up to 75 kW per rack).
120 kW-class full GPU racks: direct-to-chip cold plates; air cooling is not applicable.

blocks.p: Market confirmation: Dell'Oro Group's January 2026 report found the liquid cooling market nearly doubled in 2025 to almost $3 billion, forecast to reach approximately $7 billion by 2029.

blocks.h: 4.4 Establish baselines and acceptance criteria

blocks.p: Inference hosting carries bursty, multi-tenant load; the binding risk is tail latency, not average latency. One tenant's burst must not degrade neighboring tenants. Incast from many senders to one receiver can only be resolved by senders reducing rate; no switch creates bandwidth.
Before go-live, record baselines for four metrics: queue depth, PFC pause count, retransmission rate, and per-port error rate.

Acceptance criteria: lossless parameters verified item by item; all four baselines recorded under real load; post-launch deviation from baseline triggers investigation; a successful ping is not an acceptance criterion.

blocks.h: 5. Pre-launch checklist

ul: Classify the workload: inference or fine-tuning, versus large multi-node training. Ethernet for the former; evaluate InfiniBand separately for the latter.
Size by GPU count: under about 128 GPUs, start with tuned RoCEv2. Do not pre-purchase for a thousand-GPU future.
Confirm fabric separation: back-end, storage, front-end, and management do not share a congested link.
Verify lossless parameters item by item — PFC, ECN, DCQCN, MTU 9000, buffer depth — under real load.
Complete per-row power and cooling accounting: electrical headroom, cooling headroom, tier selection (rear-door exchanger or cold plate). Upgrade by row, not the entire hall at once.
Record the four baseline metrics and include them in routine inspection: queue depth, PFC pauses, retransmissions, port errors.

blocks.h: 6. Constraints and exceptions

ul: Large multi-node training is out of scope; fabric selection for training requires separate evaluation.
This guide does not cover migration paths for facilities with existing InfiniBand deployments.
A team that cannot yet tune Ethernet should build that capability or bring in external support before taking on inference hosting business.

blocks.h: 7. Conclusion

blocks.p: Implementation priority for small-facility AI infrastructure is, in order: Ethernet tuning, traffic isolation, and per-row power and cooling accounting. After one row is implemented and baselined, expand to the next row.

blocks.h: References

ul: Network Devices Inc., GPU Cluster Networking for On-Prem AI (2026 Guide).
Enterasource, InfiniBand vs Ethernet for AI Fabric.
NVIDIA Developer Blog, Giga-Scale AI and the Ethernet Evolution.
Uptime Institute 2025 cooling survey (786 operators).
International Energy Agency 2026 report.
